questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A.1 (Kinematics: velocity-time graphs, displacement from the area under a graph, average velocity, acceleration as the gradient)
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.1 Kinematics: reading a velocity-time graph
questions.challenge_mechanism: Every option in the cluster is a number that a defensible but incomplete reading of the same graph will produce, so nothing can be answered by pattern-matching a formula. The cluster forces the candidate to keep three distinctions apart at once: signed area against unsigned area, velocity against its gradient, and zero velocity against zero acceleration. The instant at which the object is momentarily at rest is the pivot, because the graph is still straight there and the gradient has not changed.
questions.question: The figure is the velocity-time graph for an object moving in a straight line. The object accelerates uniformly from rest, then travels at a constant velocity, then decelerates uniformly until it is momentarily at rest, and then continues to accelerate in the opposite direction. The letters A, B, C and D label the four regions between the line and the time axis: A, B and C lie above the axis and D lies below it. Because the motion is along a single straight line, the sign of the velocity gives the direction of travel, and the area between the line and the axis counts as positive displacement above the axis and negative displacement below it. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this graph, each is worth one mark, and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

figure.caption: Velocity-time graph for the motion, with the four areas A, B, C and D marked. The object reaches 9.0 m/s at t = 3.0 s, holds that velocity until t = 8.0 s, is at rest at t = 11 s, and reaches -3.0 m/s at t = 12 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the displacement of the object over the whole 12 s interval shown on the graph, taking account of the direction of travel.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The signed areas are 13.5 m, 45 m, 13.5 m and -1.5 m, and these sum to 70.5 m, so the object finishes 70.5 m from where it started.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This adds the final area as though it were positive, which gives the total distance travelled rather than the displacement.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This ignores the motion after t = 11 s altogether, summing only the three areas above the axis.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This subtracts the final triangle twice, treating its area as 3.0 m rather than the 1.5 m that the graph actually encloses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the acceleration of the object at the instant t = 11 s, at which the object is momentarily at rest.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The graph is a single straight line from t = 8 s to t = 12 s, so its gradient is (-3.0 - 9.0)/4.0 = -3.0 m s^-2 throughout, including the instant at which the velocity passes through zero.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the standard error of reading a velocity of zero as an acceleration of zero; the velocity is zero at that instant but it is changing.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This takes half of the true gradient, which would be correct only if the deceleration lasted twice as long as it does.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong, and the sign is the whole point: the object is decelerating, not accelerating forwards.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average velocity of the object over the whole 12 s interval shown on the graph.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Average velocity is the displacement divided by the time taken, so 70.5 m divided by 12 s, which is 5.88 m s^-1.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This divides the total distance travelled by the time, which gives the average speed rather than the average velocity.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This divides the displacement by 10 s, as though the motion had ended when the object first came to rest.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This removes the final area twice before dividing by 12 s, which is the same double subtraction that produces option D in part (a).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the total distance travelled by the object over the whole 12 s interval shown on the graph.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Every area is counted as positive, so the distance is 13.5 + 45 + 13.5 + 1.5 = 73.5 m, which is 3.0 m more than the displacement.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the displacement, which cancels the final 1.5 m instead of adding it, so it undercounts the ground covered by 3.0 m.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This ignores the final second of motion entirely, as though the object stopped at t = 11 s instead of reversing.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This treats the final triangle as enclosing 3.0 m rather than 1.5 m, which doubles the contribution of the last second.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Determine the speed of the object at the instant t = 9.5 s.

options.label: A
options.rationale: From t = 8 s to t = 11 s the velocity falls linearly from 9.0 m s^-1 to zero, so at t = 9.5 s it has fallen by 3.0 x 1.5 = 4.5 m s^-1, leaving 4.5 m s^-1.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This takes the deceleration to run from 8 s to 12 s rather than to 11 s, which spreads the same change in velocity over four seconds instead of three.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This quotes the magnitude of the acceleration as though it were the speed at that instant.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This keeps the velocity at its value at t = 8 s and ignores the deceleration that has already taken place by t = 9.5 s.

questions.answer:
**(a) A.** The displacement is the signed area between the graph and the time axis. From 0 to 3.0 s the region is a triangle, $\frac{1}{2}(3.0)(9.0) = 13.5$ m; from 3.0 s to 8.0 s it is a rectangle, $(5.0)(9.0) = 45$ m; from 8.0 s to 11 s it is a triangle, $\frac{1}{2}(3.0)(9.0) = 13.5$ m; from 11 s to 12 s it is a triangle below the axis, $\frac{1}{2}(1.0)(-3.0) = -1.5$ m. Adding, $13.5 + 45 + 13.5 - 1.5 = 70.5$ m. **(A1)**

**(b) A.** The acceleration is the gradient of the graph. From 8.0 s to 12 s the graph is one straight line, so the gradient is constant over that whole interval and is $(v_{12} - v_8)/(12 - 8) = (-3.0 - 9.0)/4.0 = -3.0$ m s$^{-2}$. The velocity happens to be zero at t = 11 s, but that says nothing about the gradient: the object is passing through rest, not sitting at it. **(A1)**

**(c) A.** Average velocity is displacement divided by time, $70.5/12 = 5.875$, i.e. 5.88 m s$^{-1}$. **(A1)**

**(d) A.** Distance travelled treats every area as positive, so $13.5 + 45 + 13.5 + 1.5 = 73.5$ m. The difference between this and the answer to (a) is twice the final area, 3.0 m, which is the ground covered while moving backwards and then given up again. **(A1)**

**(e) A.** On 8.0 s to 11 s the velocity falls at 3.0 m s$^{-2}$, so $v(9.5) = 9.0 - 3.0(9.5 - 8.0) = 9.0 - 4.5 = 4.5$ m s$^{-1}$. Since the velocity is still positive there, the speed equals the velocity. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark per question, no negative marking, and no method marks: the key is the answer. (a) Accept 70.5 m. The distractors are all arithmetic consequences of a defensible misreading, so a candidate who answers B has found the distance and a candidate who answers C has stopped the motion at t = 11 s. (b) This is the hardest question in the cluster and the one most often failed: accept only -3.0 m s$^{-2}$. An answer of 0 m s$^{-2}$ is the error the question exists to detect, because it confuses a zero value of the function with a zero value of its gradient. (c) Accept 5.88 m s$^{-1}$. An answer of 6.13 m s$^{-1}$ is the average speed and shows the candidate has not separated the two averages. (d) Accept 73.5 m. (e) Accept 4.5 m s$^{-1}$; accept -4.5 m s$^{-1}$ only if the candidate has explicitly read the gradient as positive, since the question asks for speed and the velocity at 9.5 s is positive. Where a candidate's two answers to (a) and (d) differ by exactly 3.0 m, the pair is internally consistent and both are likely to be right.
questions.explanation:
A velocity-time graph is worth more than the formula it encodes, and this cluster is built to make that visible. The single graph carries four pieces of information that candidates routinely run together, and each question isolates one of them.

The first distinction is between signed and unsigned area. The region D lies below the time axis, so it represents motion in the negative direction, and the displacement it contributes is negative. Distance travelled, by contrast, counts every area as positive. Parts (a) and (d) ask for the two quantities and differ by exactly twice the final triangle, 3.0 m. A candidate who gets (a) and (d) both right understands the distinction; a candidate who gets (d) right and (a) wrong has found the distance when asked for the displacement.

The second distinction is between a quantity and its rate of change. At t = 11 s the object is momentarily at rest, and the tempting answer to part (b) is that the acceleration is zero because the velocity is. That is wrong, and the graph shows why: the line is straight from t = 8 s all the way to t = 12 s, so the gradient, and therefore the acceleration, is the same at t = 11 s as it is at t = 9 s. The object does not pause at rest; it passes through. This is the same error as assuming that a ball thrown vertically upwards has zero acceleration at the top of its flight.

The third distinction is between the two averages. Average velocity uses displacement, average speed uses distance, and because the object reverses, the two differ. Part (c) asks for the velocity and offers the speed as a distractor.

Part (e) checks whether the candidate can read an intermediate value off the graph rather than only its endpoints, and the distractors correspond to reading the deceleration as ending at t = 12 s instead of t = 11 s, which is the commonest way to misplace the zero crossing.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. The figure was generated from the same segment endpoints the answers use, so the areas and the drawn line cannot disagree. The distractor set was built from the four errors this graph invites: unsigned area, velocity read as gradient, distance used as displacement, and the deceleration read as ending at the wrong time.

verification.method: Every area, gradient and derived quantity recomputed in Python from the four segment endpoints used to draw the figure, so that the picture and the arithmetic share one source; each distractor confirmed to be the exact result of the named error.
solution_skeleton: split the graph into its four straight segments and find each enclosed area
attach the sign of each area from whether it lies above or below the time axis
add the signed areas for displacement and the unsigned ones for distance
read the gradient of the relevant straight segment for the acceleration
divide displacement by the total time for the average velocity

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Read the graph crossing the time axis at t = 11 s as the point where the acceleration is zero, and take the distance travelled to be the signed area under the graph.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: From 8.0 s to 12 s the graph is a single straight line, so the gradient - and therefore the acceleration - is -3.0 m s^-2 at t = 11 s. Zero velocity does not imply zero acceleration: the object is passing through rest rather than sitting at it. Separately, the signed area gives 70.5 m, which is the displacement, whereas the ground covered is 73.5 m; the two differ by twice the final triangle.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: An acceleration of zero at t = 11 s, and a distance of 70.5 m in place of 73.5 m because the signed area is reused for the unsigned quantity.
